strengths: Well-motivated central idea: rather than treating compositionality as a byproduct of data scale, the paper explicitly controls the distribution of compositional complexity (k) in visual instruction tuning data, addressing a clearly documented 'complexity cliff' in LLaVA-665K (90% of questions require ≤2 capabilities).

The four-step data generation pipeline (capability sampling, conversation generation, quality verification, dataset assembly) is clearly described and includes concrete quality-control mechanisms (confidence thresholds, duplicate filtering, capability verification).
Strong data efficiency results: matching or exceeding full LLaVA-665K performance with ~10% of the data budget, with particularly large gains on high-complexity subsets of MMStar and MM-Vet.

Extensive and informative ablation studies: balancing k-distribution vs. matching LLaVA's skewed distribution, leave-one-out analysis of atomic capabilities, effect of compositional complexity range, and instruction-tuning-data mixing ratio all provide useful insight into why the method works.
Reasonably broad benchmark suite (8 benchmarks) covering diverse vision-centric skills, plus honest discussion of limited gains on knowledge-intensive benchmarks (OK-VQA, MMMU) in the appendix.
Plans to release the generated dataset, aiding reproducibility of the data itself (though not the generation pipeline).
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: the same closed-source model (Gemini-2.0-Flash) is used to define the capability taxonomy, generate and verify training questions, and also to retroactively assign k-labels to benchmark questions for the complexity-stratified analysis (Fig. 4). This makes the compositional-generalization claims partly self-referential and vulnerable to systematic bias from a single model's notion of 'capabilities.'

Only one base model/architecture (LLaVA-v1.5-7B with LoRA) is evaluated; there is no test of whether the compositional tuning recipe transfers to larger or more modern MLLM backbones (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, Cambrian), limiting claims of general applicability.

High-k evaluation subsets (k=4, k=5) are likely very small in absolute sample count (especially for MM-Vet/MMStar), so the large relative improvements (83–94%) may carry high variance; no confidence intervals, standard deviations across seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere in the paper.

Baselines are limited to random subsampling and ICONS; no comparison to other recent data-efficient or compositional-training approaches, nor to simply reweighting existing VIT data by capability without new generation.

Heavy dependence on a costly, closed-source proprietary model (Gemini) for every stage of the pipeline (generation, verification, and evaluation labeling) raises reproducibility concerns, which the authors acknowledge but do not mitigate with open alternatives or robustness checks.
The atomic capability taxonomy (10 categories) is manually curated and somewhat subjective; no analysis of sensitivity to different taxonomies or capability granularity is provided.

Data generation is capped at k=3 due to claimed unreliability of the generator at higher complexity, yet the paper still evaluates and touts generalization to k=4/5 without deeper investigation of why/how this generalization occurs mechanistically.

Some benchmark gains are quite modest (e.g., MME performance is actually lower than full VIT, CV-Bench also lower), which is not sufficiently discussed relative to the overall positive framing in the abstract/intro.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: VIT datasets are dominated by low-compositional-complexity (k=1) examples, and the paper quantifies this complexity cliff (90% of LLaVA-665K questions require ≤2 capabilities).

Clean, systematic four-step data generation pipeline (capability sampling, generation, verification, assembly) with a well-defined taxonomy of 10 atomic visual capabilities grouped into Attribution/Recognition/Relation.
Strong data efficiency result: matching or slightly exceeding full LLaVA-665K performance using only ~10% of the data, with clear improvements on complex multi-capability benchmarks (MM-Vet, MMStar).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of balanced complexity distribution (vs. unbalanced control matching LLaVA's k-distribution), the range of k included in training, individual capability importance (leave-one-out), and the instruction/compositional data mixing ratio.
Demonstrates generalization to compositional complexities (k=4, k=5) not explicitly present in training data, which is a meaningful signal of compositional generalization rather than memorization.

Transparent about limitations (reliance on closed-source Gemini for data generation/verification, weaker gains on knowledge-intensive tasks) and commits to releasing generated data for reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single base architecture (LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA); it is unclear whether the compositional tuning benefits transfer to other/larger MLLM backbones (e.g., 13B models, more recent architectures like Cambrian or Eagle mentioned in related work but never tested).

Potential evaluation circularity: Gemini-2.0-Flash is used both to generate/verify training data and to label the compositional complexity (k) of benchmark questions used for the generalization analysis in §4.3/Fig.4, which could bias the reported gains toward COMPACT's own notion of compositionality.

No reported sample counts for high-k subsets (k=4, k=5) of MM-Vet/MMStar; these are likely very small slices of already small benchmarks, so the large relative improvements (83.3%, 94.0%) may not be statistically robust.

Limited comparison scope: only Random and ICONS are used as data-selection baselines; no comparison to other recent data-efficient or compositionality-focused VIT recipes, nor to simply up-weighting existing rare high-k LLaVA examples instead of generating new synthetic data.

No human evaluation of the quality/naturalness of generated compositional questions—the quality verification relies entirely on the same Gemini model, raising concerns about systematic biases or errors propagating undetected into training data.
Mixed results on some benchmarks (e.g., CV-Bench, MME) where COMPACT underperforms the full VIT baseline, which somewhat tempers the “comparable across all benchmarks” claim in the abstract.
The atomic capability taxonomy (10 categories) is derived heuristically from prior literature without a rigorous justification of completeness or non-redundancy beyond the leave-one-out ablation.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated central idea: using compositional complexity (k-value) as a controllable axis for informative VIT data curation, moving beyond scale-only or influence-based selection.

Strong empirical results: with only 10% of LLaVA-665K data, COMPACT matches/exceeds full-data performance and outperforms multiple state-of-the-art data selection baselines (ICONS, SemDeDup, D2-Pruning, EL2N, etc.) on aggregate.

Thorough set of ablations and controlled analyses: matching LLaVA's k-distribution to isolate the complexity effect (Table 3), varying kgen ranges (Fig. 4), varying instruction-tuning mixture ratio (Fig. 5), per-capability ablations (Table 7), and per-k-value breakdowns on MMStar/TextVQA that support the causal claim that complexity drives gains.
Reasonable and transparent data-quality pipeline with explicit filtering criteria, and detailed failure-mode/rejection-rate analysis in the appendix.
Additional experiment with an open-source generator (Qwen3-VL-4B) shows the recipe is not entirely dependent on proprietary Gemini, partially addressing reproducibility concerns.

Useful auxiliary analyses such as token-efficiency comparisons and identification of zero-capability/noisy samples in the original LLaVA-665K dataset, which are of independent interest to the community.
weaknesses: All main experiments use a single base model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA) and single source dataset (LLaVA-665K); given the field has moved to much larger and more diverse VIT corpora (Cambrian-10M, Eagle 2), it is unclear whether the approach and gains generalize to larger backbones, other architectures, or bigger/newer instruction datasets.

The k-value complexity metric and its measurement rely on the same family of generator model (Gemini-2.0-Flash) used to both create and verify/label the data, raising concerns about circularity and self-consistency bias inflating the perceived quality/complexity gains.

Gains are not uniform across benchmarks: COMPACT underperforms the full-data baseline on CV-Bench, MME, and TextVQA (Table 2), and the paper's headline 100.2% relative performance is somewhat driven by a few benchmarks (InfoVQA, MM-Vet) while others show modest or negative deltas.

The complexity measure (count of coarse capability labels) is fairly coarse and does not rigorously capture semantic/reasoning difficulty; the taxonomy is acknowledged to be non-orthogonal and only a 'practical starting point', which weakens the theoretical grounding of the central 'k-value' contribution.
No variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for the main comparisons, making it hard to assess the significance of relatively small percentage-point differences between methods.

The paper's core insight (complex, information-dense questions are more sample-efficient than simple ones) is intuitive and has been explored in related compositionality literature; the primary novel contribution is largely an engineering pipeline for synthetic data generation rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

Reliance on costly proprietary API calls for data generation (even if described as feasible at current scale) may limit reproducibility and scalability to substantially larger data budgets than demonstrated (32K-65K samples).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing of VIT data curation via compositional 'atomic capabilities' and a quantifiable complexity metric (k-value), which is intuitive and provides new insight into why some VIT samples are more informative than others.

Extensive empirical comparison against a wide range of relevant data-selection baselines (EL2N, Perplexity, SemDeDup, D2-Pruning, Self-Sup, Self-Filter, ICONS) under matched data budgets, showing consistent gains.

Careful ablation that disentangles the effect of increased complexity from the effect of using a different data generator/distribution (COMPACT_llava experiment matching LLaVA's k-distribution), which strengthens the causal claim that complexity itself drives improvement.

Thorough appendix analyses: k-value vs. task difficulty on TextVQA, per-category MMStar breakdown, per-capability ablation, token-efficiency analysis, failure-mode/rejection-rate analysis, and an additional experiment using an open-source generator (Qwen3-VL) to address reproducibility concerns about reliance on Gemini.

Practical significance: reports strong data efficiency (90% data reduction while matching or slightly exceeding full VIT performance on average), which is a meaningful contribution to efficient MLLM training.
Good use of scaling curves (Fig. 3) showing compositional data scales more sample-efficiently than random VIT data across multiple benchmarks.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single, relatively dated backbone (LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA), making it unclear whether the benefits of complexity-aware data generation generalize to stronger, more modern MLLM architectures or to full fine-tuning rather than LoRA.

Performance is mixed rather than uniformly positive: COMPACT underperforms the full LLaVA-665K baseline noticeably on CV-Bench (55.28 vs 60.92) and LLaVA-in-the-Wild (64.50 vs 68.50); the headline 'relative performance' aggregate can mask these regressions, especially since CV-Bench is a spatial-reasoning benchmark that would seem well aligned with the paper's stated goals.

The atomic capability taxonomy (10 capabilities) is manually curated and acknowledged by the authors to be non-orthogonal and non-exhaustive, which somewhat undermines the rigor of the 'atomic' framing and the k-value as a precise complexity measure.

The complexity/quality pipeline depends heavily on judgments from a single proprietary VLM (Gemini-2.0-Flash) for capability sampling, question generation, and verification, introducing potential circularity (the same model both creates and verifies compositional correctness) and possible biases/errors that are only partially mitigated by the open-source generator ablation.
Gains on knowledge-intensive benchmarks (OK-VQA, MMMU, MMMU-Pro) are modest, limiting the generality of the compositional-tuning approach beyond narrowly vision-centric tasks.

The data generation process is costly and API-dependent, which the authors acknowledge as a reproducibility concern; while data release is promised, the pipeline itself (prompts, iterative verification) is complex and may be difficult to exactly reproduce or extend to new domains.

Scale of experiments is relatively small (up to 65K total training samples); it remains unclear whether the observed efficiency gains persist or diminish when scaling compositional tuning data toward the sizes used by modern large-scale VIT corpora (e.g., Cambrian-10M, Eagle 2).
